content: Respiratory disease is the primary cause of illness and death in individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF). To manage respiratory symptoms, various therapies are employed, including bronchodilator therapy, which aims to alleviate shortness of breath and facilitate airway opening to aid mucus clearance. Despite the widespread use of inhaled bronchodilators in CF, there is limited objective evidence supporting their effectiveness. A previous Cochrane Review that evaluated both shortand long-acting inhaled bronchodilators for CF was withdrawn in 2016. This review has since been replaced by two separate reviews: one focusing on long-acting inhaled bronchodilators and the other, which is the subject of this discussion, focusing on short-acting inhaled bronchodilators. The term inhaled in this context encompasses the use of pressurized metered-dose inhalers (MDIs), with or without spacers, dry powder inhalers, and nebulizers. The objective of this review was to assess the clinical outcomes and safety of short-acting inhaled bronchodilators in both children and adults with CF. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, which includes data from electronic databases and hand-searched journals and conference abstracts. The search was last updated on March 28, 2022, with additional searches of trial registries for new or ongoing studies conducted on April 12, 2022. References from relevant articles and reviews were also examined. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs that evaluated the effects of any short-acting inhaled bronchodilator, delivered via any device, at any dose, frequency, or duration, compared to either placebo or another short-acting inhaled bronchodilator in individuals with CF. Standard Cochrane methodology was used to screen references. Two authors independently extracted data and assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane RoB 1 tool. When data could not be included in the analysis, results were reported directly from the original studies. The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. The review included 11 trials with a total of 191 participants who met the inclusion criteria. Three of these trials had three treatment arms. Eight trials compared short-acting inhaled beta-2 agonists to placebo, while four trials compared short-acting inhaled muscarinic antagonists to placebo. Three trials compared short-acting inhaled beta-2 agonists to short-acting inhaled muscarinic antagonists. All trials were of a cross-over design and involved small participant numbers. Data from only three trials comparing short-acting inhaled beta-2 agonists to placebo could be included in the meta-analysis. For short-acting inhaled beta-2 agonists versus placebo, eight trials (six single-dose and two longer-term trials) reported on forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1), either as a percentage of predicted values (% predicted) or in liters (L). A meta-analysis of two trials showed a greater percentage change from baseline in FEV1 (L) after beta-2 agonist use compared to placebo, with a mean difference (MD) of 6% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.88 to 12.02; 2 trials, 82 participants). Only one of the longer-term trials reported on exacerbations, measured by hospitalizations and antibiotic courses. Another longer-term trial presented participant-reported outcomes. Adverse events were narratively reported in three trials, and all were mild. Forced vital capacity (FVC) was reported in three single-dose trials and two longer-term trials, while peak expiratory flow (FEF25-75) was reported in five trials. One trial assessed airway clearance by measuring sputum weight. The certainty of evidence for all these outcomes was judged to be very low, indicating significant uncertainty regarding the effects of short-acting inhaled beta-2 agonists. For short-acting inhaled muscarinic antagonists versus placebo, four trials evaluated the effects of ipratropium bromide, using different doses and delivery methods. One trial reported FEV1 as % predicted, while three trials measured it in liters. Two trials reported adverse events, which were few and mild. FVC was reported in one trial, and FEF25-75 was reported in three trials. None of the trials assessed quality of life, exacerbations, or airway clearance. The certainty of evidence for all outcomes was judged to be very low, indicating substantial uncertainty about the effects of short-acting inhaled muscarinic antagonists. For short-acting inhaled beta-2 agonists versus short-acting inhaled muscarinic antagonists, three single-dose trials were included, but none provided analyzable data. The original reports from these trials indicated that both treatments improved FEV1 (L). Only one trial reported on adverse events, and no participants experienced any. None of the trials reported on other outcomes of interest. The certainty of evidence for this comparison was also judged to be very low, reflecting considerable uncertainty about the relative effects of these two types of bronchodilators. In conclusion, the included trials were small and employed a cross-over design. Most studies focused on the short-term effects of inhaled bronchodilators and did not evaluate long-term outcomes. The certainty of evidence across all outcomes was very low, preventing any definitive conclusions about the effects of short-acting inhaled bronchodilators in individuals with CF.
